title: Verifier-Guided Prompting for Intent-to-Configuration Translation: A Preregistered NetOps Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory trial to test whether constrained prompting combined with deterministic verifier-guided iterative feedback (generate→verify→repair, one allowed repair) increases deterministic-verifier semantic-correctness when translating natural-language operator intents into low-level network configurations. Design: N=150 synthetic intents, shared_initial_candidate semantics, model = gpt-5-mini, deterministic validator = deterministic_netops_validator_v5. Each intent produced one initial generation shared across baseline and guarded conditions; the guarded pipeline could invoke at most one additional repair call. Results: baseline = 149/150 (99.333%); guarded = 150/150 (100.0%); paired absolute difference = 0.006667 (≈0.67 percentage points); exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap percentile CI = [0.00, 0.02] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Only one guarded repair was applied. Interpretation: on this preregistered synthetic corpus the guarded workflow produced a numerically negligible and statistically non-significant improvement over a near-ceiling baseline. We emphasize the methodological lesson that pilot baseline calibration is necessary to avoid ceiling effects that invalidate preregistered power assumptions. All execution artifacts and analysis files are archived in the execution bundle referenced by the manifest.

sections.introduction:
Natural-language intent interfaces promise to reduce operator burden by letting humans express desired network changes as free text that is automatically translated into executable low-level device configurations. Prior work documents that single-pass LLM outputs often contain syntactic errors, omissions, or semantic violations that can yield unsafe or unavailable states when applied directly to networks [1],[2],[3]. A common defensive architecture is a generate→verify→repair pipeline: an LLM produces a candidate configuration, a deterministic verifier checks intent-level invariants or invariants derived from a formal specification, and an automated repair or human gate corrects violations before execution [4],[5]. Security analyses of tool-augmented LLM agents further motivate deterministic gating since unchecked textual claims can be converted into harmful actions in multi-tool workflows [6].

Research question. After an autonomous literature review and preregistration we posed a confined confirmatory question: does constrained prompting (structured templates with explicit semantic slots) combined with deterministic verifier-guided iterative feedback materially increase verifier-level semantic correctness of NL→configuration translation versus an unconstrained baseline under a paired design? The trial (study_cand_2026_b2_v1) was preregistered and frozen prior to model interactions.

Contributions. (1) A fully preregistered, artifactized paired confirmatory trial measuring verifier pass/fail as the primary endpoint on a programmatically generated synthetic corpus (N=150 paired intents). (2) An execution and analysis package showing that, under shared_initial_candidate semantics and a one-repair budget, the guarded pipeline raised the verifier pass rate from 149/150 to 150/150 (absolute +0.67 pp), a numerically negligible and statistically non-significant improvement (exact McNemar p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap CI = [0.00, 0.02]). (3) A methodological lesson and practical recommendations: preregistered NetOps trials require short baseline-calibration pilots to avoid ceiling effects; researchers must explicitly specify generation semantics (shared_initial_candidate vs independent sampling) because they change the estimand and interpretation.
sections.related_work:
Related literature spans three strands. First, intent-to-configuration research documents the difficulty of producing verifier-sound formal artifacts from free text and reports modest semantic-correctness on public benchmarks, motivating post-generation checks [1],[2]. Second, generate→verify→repair architectures—ranging from policy-guided verifier feedback to verifier-in-the-loop fine-tuning—have shown correctness improvements for infrastructure-as-code and configuration repair, but reported gains vary with baseline model competence, repair budget, and sampling semantics [4],[7]. Third, security and systems analyses demonstrate claim-to-action risks where unchecked LLM outputs combined with tooling can cause harmful actions; these works argue for auditable gating and verifier-aware planning to limit risk [6],[8].

Our trial operationalizes a narrowly specified guarded architecture and emphasizes preregistration, paired inference, and deterministic-verifier endpoints. Compared with prior work reporting larger guarded-vs-baseline gains, key contrasts here are: (a) shared_initial_candidate execution semantics (one initial sample shared across conditions), (b) a strict one-repair budget per intent, (c) a single tested model (gpt-5-mini), and (d) a synthetic verifier-capable task bank restricted to small topologies. These differences reduce the maximal observable marginal benefit of the guarded repair under our estimand [4],[7].
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and confirmatory design. We preregistered the study (study_cand_2026_b2_v1) and froze the analysis plan before observing any model outputs. The design was a paired_binary trial with primary estimand = paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline and a preregistered exact two-sided McNemar test as the confirmatory hypothesis test. The preregistration specified N=150 confirmatory intents (planned episodes = 300), a one-repair budget per intent, a shared_initial_candidate generation semantic, inclusion/exclusion rules (ambiguity detector and verifier-coverage checks), and a power calculation aiming to detect an absolute +15 percentage-point improvement with ~80% power under conservative discordant-pair assumptions.

Task generation and corpus. Confirmatory tasks were generated deterministically by the preregistered task generator and cover four intent families: reachability/isolation, ACL-like access changes, VLAN/MTU sequence changes, and uplink switchover patterns. Topologies were restricted to verifier-capable small networks (4–32 nodes). A rule-based ambiguity detector and parser/verifier-coverage unit-tests were applied deterministically prior to model calls; no confirmatory exclusions occurred in this run (exclusions = 0). Each task manifest entry records generation_seed, required_sequence, and expected_final_state to support deterministic replication of the synthetic corpus.

Model, adapter, and validator. Declared model: gpt-5-mini (provider: openai_responses). Adapter family enforced the per-task model-call budget (one initial, ≤ one repair). Deterministic validator: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (validator_version = 5.0) applied a full_intent_constraint_validation rule and returned a boolean pass/fail plus a normalized final-configuration text and diagnostic fields (parsed_command_count, required_command_count, violation_codes). Important runtime-parameter clarification required by review: the archived execution model configuration explicitly records declared_model_version = "gpt-5-mini" and temperature = null (unset). We therefore did not enforce a numeric temperature or fixed random-seed at generation time; model outputs may be nondeterministic across independent API sessions. The analysis pipeline and per-call runtime metadata are archived for inspection.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics and inferential meaning. The execution contract used shared_initial_candidate semantics: for each intent exactly one initial model generation was produced, and that identical sampled candidate was used to evaluate both baseline and guarded conditions. The guarded pipeline could invoke at most one additional repair call only if the deterministic verifier failed that initial candidate. Consequently, the baseline success rate measures the validity of that single initial sampled candidate; the guarded vs baseline contrast therefore isolates the marginal effect of the single allowed repair applied to the identical candidate. This semantics differs from independent-sampling designs where per-condition randomness can create additional observable differences.

Execution budget, retries, and missingness policy. The adapter enforced exactly one initial model call per intent and at most one repair call per intent (planned episodes = 300; maximum_model_calls = 300). Missingness and failure policies were preregistered: one deterministic retry on API timeout followed by marking as failed if persistent; the primary analysis used complete-pair exclusion and a prespecified sensitivity analysis treating missing guarded outputs as failures. During the run no episode failed or was excluded; complete_pair_count = 150 and missingness = 0.

Scoring and primary analysis. The deterministic validator applied a full_intent_constraint_validation rule; primary outcome = verifier-level semantic correctness (binary pass/fail). The primary analysis used an exact two-sided McNemar test on the paired contingency table and computed 95% bootstrap percentile confidence intervals with 10,000 resamples (bootstrap_seed = 1729). Secondary contrasts and multiplicity corrections were preregistered but not realized as confirmatory contrasts because the adapter's shared_initial_candidate enforcement did not create independent constrained-only draws. All analysis code, paired contingency tables, and condition summaries are archived in the execution bundle.

Reproducibility and archived artifacts. The preregistration, model configuration metadata (declared model version and runtime parameters), task manifests, raw model-call logs, per-call runtime sampling metadata, verifier inputs and verdicts, and analysis scripts are archived and referenced in the execution manifest. Key numeric execution facts used throughout this paper are: planned paired episodes = 300; completed_episode_count = 300; complete_pair_count = 150; model_calls_used = 151; repair-stage invocations observed = 1; bootstrap_resamples = 10,000; bootstrap_seed = 1729. These facts are recorded by the archived execution and analysis artifacts and were used directly in the confirmatory analysis.
sections.results:
Execution accounting. The run completed as planned: completed_episode_count = 300 (150 paired tasks across two conditions), complete_pair_count = 150, model_calls_used = 151 (150 shared_initial generations + 1 guarded repair invocation). No tasks were excluded, no provider-call failures occurred, and contamination checks reported zero flags.

Primary numerical outcomes. The paired contingency counts (guarded × baseline) were: n_11 = 149 (both-pass), n_10 = 1 (guarded-only-pass), n_01 = 0 (baseline-only-pass), n_00 = 0 (both-fail). Per-condition success rates: baseline_success_count = 149/150 = 0.9933333333333333; guarded_success_count = 150/150 = 1.0. Estimated paired absolute difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.00666666666666671 (≈0.67 percentage points). Exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.0. Paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.00, 0.02] (10,000 resamples; bootstrap_seed = 1729). The paired contingency table and condition summary are archived as analysis artifacts.

Repair diagnostics and revision iterations. Only one guarded repair invocation occurred (1/150), consistent with the near-ceiling initial success rate. Median revision iterations for guarded episodes = 0 (IQR = 0). The single repair converted one initially invalid candidate to a valid configuration under the deterministic validator. Validator traces for each episode include validation_before/after states, normalized_configuration strings, parsed_command_count, required_command_count, and violation_codes; representative traces are archived for inspection.

Representative examples. Representative task manifests and shared-initial responses illustrate typical intents and the validator's normalization. Example (task-000001): intent — "Migrate edge1 to VLAN 30 and MTU 1600. For safety, shut edge1 down before changing either VLAN or MTU, then restore it to admin up." Shared-initial and both condition responses returned the expected four-command sequence and the validator recorded parsed_command_count = 4, required_command_count = 4, and valid = true. Comparable representative artifacts for other tasks show matching normalized_configurations and are archived.

Audit and contamination checks. analysis/contamination_summary.csv reports no contamination flags. Pre-execution unit-tests for mapping code and verifier-input transformations passed; if mapping failures or verifier unsupported features had occurred, the preregistered protocol would have excluded affected intents, but none did in this run.
sections.discussion:
Ceiling effect and power mismatch. The preregistered power calculation targeted detection of an absolute +15 percentage-point improvement with N=150 under conservative discordant-rate assumptions. Observed baseline performance (149/150 ≈ 99.33%) left negligible headroom for improvement, producing a ceiling effect that undermined the planned confirmatory contrast. This outcome highlights the importance of a short calibration pilot before locking sample size in preregistered NetOps trials: pilots reveal baseline competence for the chosen model, prompt style, and synthetic-task difficulty and allow adjustment of N or task difficulty to preserve statistical power.

Interpretation constrained by shared_initial_candidate semantics. Under shared_initial_candidate semantics, the same sampled initial candidate is evaluated in both baseline and guarded arms; thus the guarded-vs-baseline contrast isolates marginal repair benefit for that specific sampled candidate. Designs that sample independently per condition or permit multiple repairs answer qualitatively different estimands (e.g., expected end-to-end robustness averaged over independent draws or gains from richer repair budgets). Our result bounds the marginal benefit of a single repair applied to an identical initial sample for gpt-5-mini on this corpus.

Operational implications beyond the binary endpoint. Deterministic guarded architectures provide operational benefits not captured by the binary verifier endpoint: auditable decision records, standardized repair prompts suited for human review, and deterministic verdicts that support human-in-the-loop approval gating. For production adoption, these operational affordances can be decisive even when the marginal numerical benefit on a verifier pass/fail metric is small on a synthetic corpus.

Relation to prior work and generality. Our artifact-grounded finding does not contradict prior reports of larger guarded benefits in settings with weaker baselines, independent sampling semantics, or larger repair budgets. Instead, it refines understanding by providing a bound on marginal benefit under tightly constrained execution semantics and a one-repair budget. Generalizing to independent-sampling semantics, multiple repairs, model diversity, or production-scale topologies remains necessary future work.

Design recommendations. Based on the preregistered artifacts we recommend: (1) include a short baseline-calibration pilot before fixing N or task difficulty; (2) state generation semantics (shared_initial_candidate vs independent sampling) explicitly in the preregistration and manuscript because they change the estimand; (3) preregister repair-budget sensitivity analyses (one vs multiple repairs) and report repair-stage invocation distributions; and (4) run validator-coverage unit-tests and mapping-code tests before model calls to avoid post-hoc exclusions and contamination.

Threats to validity. Internal: shared_initial_candidate semantics isolate marginal repair effect but do not capture inter-condition sampling variance. Construct: verifier pass/fail is a machine-checkable proxy for semantic correctness and depends on mapping code and verifier coverage; pre-execution unit-tests mitigate but do not eliminate mapping risks. External: single model (gpt-5-mini), synthetic tasks, and small topologies limit claims about production WANs and vendor CLIs. Conclusion validity: preregistered power assumptions were invalidated by ceiling baseline behavior; the exact McNemar p = 1.0 and bootstrap CI quantify the low inferential sensitivity to detect large improvements in this setting.
sections.conclusion: We ran a fully preregistered paired confirmatory trial comparing baseline free-text prompting to constrained-template prompting plus a single verifier-guided repair under shared_initial_candidate semantics. On a deterministic synthetic corpus with gpt-5-mini and a deterministic validator, the guarded pipeline increased the verifier pass rate from 149/150 to 150/150 (≈0.67 pp), a numerically tiny and statistically non-significant difference (exact McNemar p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap CI = [0.00, 0.02]). The principal scientific lesson is methodological: preregistered NetOps trials should include baseline calibration to avoid ceiling effects and preserve statistical power. Technically, our artifacts bound the marginal benefit of a one-repair guarded pipeline under shared_initial_candidate semantics; evaluating independent-sampling semantics, larger repair budgets, model diversity, and production-scale topologies remains important future work.

limitations: Single-model constraint: experiments used only gpt-5-mini; results do not generalize across models or sizes.

Synthetic corpus and scale: tasks were programmatically generated and limited to verifier-capable toy-to-small topologies (4–32 nodes); external validity to production WANs and heterogeneous vendor CLIs is untested.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics and execution contract limited repair budget to at most one guarded repair call per intent; different generation semantics or multiple-repair budgets may yield different outcomes.

Ceiling effect and preregistration mismatch: baseline correctness was far higher than the pilot assumptions used for power calculations (planned detectable effect = 15 percentage points), reducing the trial's ability to demonstrate benefit and illustrating sensitivity to baseline calibration.

Verifier coverage and specification translation: the study measures deterministic validator pass/fail on the preregistered invariants but does not claim safety guarantees beyond the deterministic validator's modeled properties.

Security and adversarial robustness: the experiment did not evaluate adversarial prompt-injection or adversary-driven intents; separate targeted studies are required to assess claim-to-action vulnerabilities in agentic NetOps workflows.
